title: Goal-owned durable events
summary: Goal state is recorded by its own durable goal/change event that carries the whole goal snapshot and is appended by the goal service; it is no longer encoded inside an inbox message.
firstReason: A domain's durable state should not depend on message scheduling; keep the domain-owned whole-value event.

title: One output ring, one projection, one event stream for background jobs
summary: Each background job has one output ring that serves both the model's consuming read and observers' offset reads, plus one projection and one event stream; this replaced duplicated vocabularies and listener families.
firstReason: One store with two cursors is the simpler and correct shape; keep it.

title: Host-owned scheduled messages
summary: Scheduled messages live in a host-owned storage domain, not in a session, so they survive restart and fire while the target session is not loaded. The store is authoritative: an unreadable or invalid file is a load failure and is never read as 'no tasks'.
firstReason: A timer attached to a live agent cannot wake a session that is not loaded, in any language. The fail-closed load rule prevents a corrupt file from silently deleting reminders. The version 1 read compatibility in the note is not needed (DH-ADR-2).

title: Standalone schedules and Session targets
summary: A schedule delivers to one of three targets: an existing session, a session created once at first delivery, or a new session per delivery. Session ids are reserved before each create attempt, so a retry after a failed delivery reuses the same session.
firstReason: Reserving the id before the attempt is what makes a delivery retry safe (no duplicate sessions). The target model and the title rule for created sessions are product behaviour.

title: Schedule deletes task rows and bounds delivery history
summary: Deleting a schedule removes its row and its delivery records; there is no 'deleted' state and no recycle bin. Delivery history is bounded by age (default 30 days) and count (default 200), applied on the only write path.
firstReason: Soft delete added a state every reader had to skip, and unbounded history made each rewrite of the task grow. Both rules are storage design, independent of language.

title: Preset-scoped Schedule tools
summary: The model-facing schedule tools are a separate plugin mounted per agent preset; the schedule service itself stays host-wide. A preset that does not mount the tools pays no prompt tokens for their schemas.
firstReason: Registering tools from the service attached them to every root agent, including the minimal preset. Splitting a host service from its model-facing consumer is a pattern the Go composition should follow for every capability.

title: Delivered reminders are framed as scheduled messages from the user
summary: A delivered reminder is a user-role message that opens with a fixed line saying it is a scheduled message from the user. The earlier wording that told the model to treat the payload as untrusted was removed.
firstReason: A message cannot credibly declare its own content untrusted, and the model may have written the prompt itself. Stating only the origin is accurate. Prompt wording is independent of the implementation language.

title: Schedule rule storage and shared recurrence
summary: There is one schedule storage domain. Cron expressions and recurrence rules are ordinary timing kinds in it, with parsing and occurrence arithmetic in the shared time package, and there is no second store or importer.
firstReason: A parallel store with an importer duplicated timing and storage authority. The Go design starts with one domain; the version 1 read compatibility is not needed (DH-ADR-2).

title: Persist owned job lifecycle facts
summary: Jobs owned by a session append `job/registered` and `job/settled` facts to the session log, with timestamps, owner, producer kind and a UUID job id that survives registry restarts. The settled fact says whether the producer reported completion or the bookkeeping was forced, and a failed journal append warns but never blocks cleanup.
firstReason: Without logged facts an SDK consumer cannot reconstruct when background work actually ran. It follows the event-sourced session model the Go design keeps.

title: Model-facing same-session goal tools
summary: Three exclusive tools, `get_goal`, `create_goal` and `update_goal`, let the model read, create and change a long-running goal in its own session. Updates are compare-and-set on goal id and revision, and resuming a paused goal is reserved for the user.
firstReason: The compare-and-set contract and the authority rule (who may resume) prevent stale or unauthorized goal changes whatever the host language.

title: Archive admission reads the stored tasks
summary: The schedule provider answers archive admission from the stored task rows, not from a live agent, and a stop deletes those rows in one batch on the same serialized queue the tools use. An idle or cold session with armed reminders therefore refuses the archive.
firstReason: Answering from stored state closes the gap in which a session with no live agent could be archived while its reminders still fire. Ordering the delete behind creates that are still in flight is a concurrency rule Go must keep.

title: Explicit Schedule time-zone boundary
summary: The browser's time zone is sampled with every prompt and logged on that user message; it is never stored as session state. The schedule tool accepts only a time with an explicit offset or an explicit zone, and the model is told to ask the user when the zone is mixed or missing.
firstReason: Making the zone explicit removed session headers, migrations and a confirmation protocol. The rule carries over; the server-rendered UI needs one line of script to put the browser's zone into the prompt form.

title: Event-triggered automation tasks
summary: Proposal: an automation task becomes an instruction plus a source and a session mode, and time is only one source. A source provider (code, no model) reports changes; a shared trigger compares each observation with stored state and filters it, still without a model call; only a change that passes is delivered to a session, where the event content is quoted as data from the source and not as the user's words.
firstReason: Adopt the layering, not necessarily the build order. The two problems it solves, a model turn per poll and untrusted event text reaching the model as if the user wrote it, are independent of the language, and source providers fit compiled-in components or plugin processes. The schedule area should shape task storage so that time is one source among several, and may give the event sources a later priority.
